chapters.title: Evolution Begins with Change: Turbulence Brings Far More Opportunity Than Threat
chapters.summary: After the Level 3 alert, consumers hold “higher expectations.” Brands shift among four quadrants of playing to win or not to lose; digitally strong firms were hit less.

chapters.title: Building Corporate Resilience: Shaping the Keys to Survival
chapters.summary: Resilience takes both talent and digital skills; tools without a mindset shift waste money. Examples: Nike, “The New York Times,” Nan Shan Life's coaching program.

chapters.title: Building Social Impact
chapters.summary: A logic model separates Output, Outcome, and Impact to plan social engagement, with Dentsu's four-year “Take Off, Little Mei!” town-building in Laomei as the example.

chapters.title: Seizing the Home Commerce Opportunity
chapters.summary: The pandemic made home an office, gym, restaurant, and playground at once. Brands must reach into consumers' homes with experiences and restart home commerce.

chapters.title: Consumer Resources and Opportunities Hidden in the Pandemic
chapters.summary: The pandemic meant less movement, more time home, dull routine. Of six new-normal traits, strong e-commerce, sweeping promos, and instant gratification are fundamental.

chapters.title: Break the Rules, Co-Create the Ecosystem
chapters.summary: Separate needs, wants, and demands; find striking insights in people, events, time, place, things; co-create across industries, e.g. moving gym coaches and friends home.

chapters.title: “4x3” Visions of Future Life and Emotional Otherworlds
chapters.summary: From Consumer Vision 2030 and talks with 16 Taiwan experts, 2030 splits into universal advocacy, synthetic society, brand offensive, and human essence, three trends each.

chapters.title: Crossing 2030
chapters.summary: Climate, data governance, kaleidoscope self, superhumans, virtual reality, emotional tech, brand titans, happiness, star ratings, human touch, spontaneity, true faith.

chapters.title: Toward an Inclusive, Wise Era of Shared Prosperity
chapters.summary: By 2030 the 2000s generation leads spending and seeks diversity, equity, and inclusion. Brands need 5I thinking and inclusion to find value good for humanity as a whole.

chapters.title: Is Your Brand Clean Yet?
chapters.summary: Net zero replaces energy saving as the benchmark. Brands must train transparency in business, environment, and social impact; “cleansing” is sustainability evolving.

chapters.title: Media Tech Always Comes from Human Nature
chapters.summary: New media don't replace old ones; they stack. The media economy moved from traffic to content to influencers to trust. Media is just an amplifier with trust at its core.

chapters.title: Brand Value Comes from an Authenticity Consumers Believe In
chapters.summary: In a sensationalist media age, brands must tell true stories consumers believe. Examples: Dove and HONDA CR-V's “Daughter's Little Love Song.”

chapters.title: Mindset Decides Whether Data Creates Value or a Swamp
chapters.summary: With cookies gone, everyone rushes to build first-party data, but blind tech worship leads to a data swamp. Center on business goals, think long-term, start with 80/20.

chapters.title: Brand Apocalypse Now: The Era of Customer Experience Innovation
chapters.summary: Shopify and Grab grew fast on ecosystems and user insight; over a third of people would consider relying on one brand for daily needs. Better experience is brand growth.

chapters.title: Value-Driven Consumption: Brand Communication Strategy Amid Fragmented, Diverse Identities
chapters.summary: Gen Z defines itself by personality, values, and interests. Accounts with under 50K followers can spark a boycott, so brands must segment messages across diverse values.

chapters.title: Deconstructing the Kaleidoscope of Motives to Give Brand Value Concrete Form
chapters.summary: Red Bull sees itself as a culture company: its site leads with Red Bull TV and events, products last, using content to become part of consumers' lives.

chapters.title: A Wave of Emotion Is Coming: Using Tech to Seize Two-Way Opportunity
chapters.summary: The pandemic stretched health to body, mind, and spirit. Emotion-recognition tech helps people read themselves, and detects emotions ads trigger to optimize delivery.

chapters.title: The Last Mile into the New Normal
chapters.summary: Taiwanese are online nearly 8 hours a day, so in-person moments stand out. Offline big data reaches seniors; Dentsu One's running ad jersey uses beacons and face ID.

chapters.title: Commerce Architecture Under the New Paradigm
chapters.summary: The pandemic pushed online shopping 5 years ahead. Brands should use the cloud and a CDP to link data scattered across departments, building DTC around the customer.

chapters.title: The New Identity Revolution
chapters.summary: With third-party cookies gone, FLoC, Unified ID 2.0, and first-party tracking compete to set the rules. Brands should build their own identity graph.

chapters.title: Deconstructing the Consumer Journey with Search Data
chapters.summary: No cookies, but there's still search: the five ISRPE stages sort search terms by timing and need to reveal consumer intent.

chapters.title: Retail Media: The Next Wave of Emerging Media Is Here
chapters.summary: Retailers own the moment of purchase and member data, becoming media companies. Brands are now their clients and should seek self-serve, transparently priced platforms.

chapters.title: How a Story About “Trust” Won Taiwan's First Cannes Lions Grand Prix
chapters.summary: Sinyi Realty's “Trust and Happiness” film deliberately sold nothing, yet 70% of viewers rated the brand higher in post-tests. It won Taiwan's first Cannes Grand Prix.

npcs.name: Ting-ting
npcs.title: Social Media Editor, Second Year
lines: My inbox today is fuller than my life.
The comments are on fire again. Somebody save me.
I took a screenshot. Screenshotting is a social editor's instinct.
Should replies get emojis? Or will I get yelled at for that?

npcs.name: Ah-Hao
npcs.title: Marketing Contact, Steady Legs Fitness
lines: Run five kilometers today, and I've earned popcorn chicken tonight.
There are more rowing machines in our warehouse than people in our office.
If only everyone on this riverbank wore our gear.
Squats will never betray you. Inventory will.

npcs.name: Wen-wen
npcs.title: Member Media Sales, Shin Kong Mitsuki
lines: We don't just sell counter space now. We sell our members' eyeballs.
Transparent reports, transparent pricing. Only the parking lot isn't transparent.
The department store became a media company. My business card is on version three.
Anniversary-sale crowds are our TV ratings.

npcs.name: Ah-Kun
npcs.title: Runner in a Light-Up Ad Jersey
lines: The shirt on my back lights up. I'm not the one glowing.
When City Hall Station is packed, I'm a billboard that runs.
Today's goal: 30,000 steps and one sponsored post.
Don't film my face. The camera on this shirt gets you first.

missions.title: Attack or Defend
missions.brief: A supplement brand's chairman is back from a conference wanting “full digital transformation” by next week. Manager Chen waits at Taipei Wun-Zero-Wun with an AI quote.

lines.text: {role}, our chairman says times are shaky: a big sale for share, or regulars first.
Then he casually signed for an AI marketing system. NT$3M, live next month.
Who's going to use it?
My team of five. We ask each other how to make an Excel pivot table.
Same in 2021, during the Level 3 alert. We bought tools. They gathered dust in storage.
I don't want a repeat. Help me think: where do we start?

steps.prompt: The budget covers one thing. What should Manager Chen do first?

options.text: Defend: put money into current members, better after-sales and repurchase service. Keep regulars.
options.feedback: Repurchases steadied within two months. The chairman called it too timid: “What about new customers?” Manager Chen left three printed repurchase reports on his desk.
options.insight: In the book's four quadrants, Play-not-to-lose centers on existing customers: better service, lower operating risk. But the book adds that brands should switch between offense and defense as timing shifts, not pick one and freeze.

options.text: Attack: while rivals pull back, lower the membership bar and run promos to grab market share.
options.feedback: New members jump by 4,000 in a week, and so do support calls. In week three, someone on a forum asks, “Is the free sign-up jar the same as the full-price one?”
options.insight: The book says Play-to-win brands grab ground with discounts and lower membership bars, and the firms hit least by the pandemic had one thing in common: their digital development was already fairly mature.

options.text: Invest in people first: consultants coach the team for three months, learning the system on the job.
options.feedback: For three weeks everyone grumbles. In month two, someone pulls a member churn list on their own. The chairman says nothing, but approves next quarter's training budget.
options.insight: The book says resilience comes from boosting both talent and digital skills; adding tools without changing how the org thinks wastes the investment. Nan Shan Life ran a 3–6 month “digital transformation innovation coach” program on real work.

inline.q: “Building Corporate Resilience” says the value that systems and processes create depends on what?
inline.explain: Only digitally skilled users get the most from tools. “The New York Times” began shifting in 2011; digital first beat print in 2020. Biggest hurdle: culture clash inside.
inline.source: Building Corporate Resilience: Shaping the Keys to Survival

card.title: Change Minds, Then Systems
card.text: Switch offense and defense as timing shifts. What makes switching possible is people who can use the tools.

missions.title: Earth God Shrine Charity Day
missions.brief: A detergent brand wants its annual charity day on Fude St.: gift a mural, take some brand photos. Temple Uncle asks just one thing: “Will you be back next year?”

lines.text: Young one, that “Bubbles Be Gone” company wants to paint a wall, snap photos, and leave?
The proposal says a one-day event and one press release.
A few years back a bank came to plant trees. The trees died. The sign's still there.
And folks say their factory dumps wastewater in the creek. You can find it online.
It's not that they're unwelcome. People on this street just have long memories.

steps.prompt: The client decides this afternoon. What do you recommend?

options.text: Run the one-day event as planned: mural, press, volunteer group photo. Max out the coverage.
options.feedback: Twenty-some news stories run, and the client is thrilled. A month later, someone posts the mural next to old news of the factory's runoff, titled “Whitewashing One Wall.”
options.insight: The book warns that consumers see brands without net-zero goals as accomplices in environmental decline, and then no amount of image ads or PR can help.

options.text: Draw a logic model: ask what the street needs, set three-year goals, measure more than head counts.
options.feedback: An afternoon with Temple Uncle reveals the need: a place for kids after school. The client makes it a three-year story program, starting with a temple-square book nook.
options.insight: The book splits social engagement results into Output, Outcome, and Impact. Dentsu's “Take Off, Little Mei!” spent four years in Laomei, with 1,000+ staff and 25,000 hours in all, building Taiwan's first multimedia picture-book town.

options.text: Fix the factory first: publish emissions data and net-zero goals. Hold the event once there's news.
options.feedback: The client's plant manager scowls but agrees to publish data within three months. Charity day moves to next spring. Temple Uncle says, “Now that's more like it.”
options.insight: The book says truly transparent brands train three “vital stats”: transparent business operations, environmental change, and social impact. “Cleansing” is how sustainable business “evolves.”

inline.q: “Is Your Brand Clean Yet?” lists three “vital stats” of transparency brands must train. Which one is NOT among them?
inline.explain: The three are transparency in business operations, environmental change, and social impact. Ad budgets aren't on the list.

card.title: Results Come in Three Layers
card.text: How many press releases you sent is Output. Whether the street got better is Impact.

missions.title: NT$1,300 per Order
missions.brief: Meal-kit brand “Homebody Chef King” sees online order value sliding, so the owner wants a NT$3,000 bundle. From the store counter, Ning has seen how people really shop.

lines.text: {role}, see this pickup slip? One person, three pickups a week, a pack or two each.
The Homebody Chef King owner says order value fell. He wants a NT$3,000 bundle.
NT$3,000? What we hear most around here is: my freezer's full.
And people aren't too lazy to cook. They're sick of cooking the same thing every day.
My roommate bought one last week after a short video of someone chatting while cooking.

steps.prompt: The owner wants your pick this afternoon. What do you push?

options.text: Do what the owner wants: push the NT$3,000 bundle with spend-more gifts to lift order value.
options.feedback: The bundle sells well in week one. In week two, the top return reason is “won't fit in the freezer.” Support makes a freezer size chart. A little sad to read.
options.insight: The book cites National Credit Card Center data: online's share of transactions rose from 25% in Jan 2019 to 45% in Jan 2021, while average spend fell from NT$3,000 to NT$1,300. Small, frequent orders are a trend, not a glitch.

options.text: Go small and frequent: a weekly restock subscription, two or three packs, picked up at the store.
options.feedback: Subscribers show up like clockwork, and Ning learns their names. The owner grumbles the price is too low, but after seeing the repurchase rate he drops the bundle.
options.insight: The book judges that of the six new-normal traits, strong e-commerce, sweeping promotions, and instant gratification are fundamental shifts that will last; brands must follow how consumers reallocate time and money.

options.text: Solve “sick of cooking”: a weekly livestream with one new dish, the brand cooking along at home.
options.feedback: The first stream draws just 80 people; by the third, viewers post photos of their own dishes. You spend three straight Thursday nights typing in the chat.
options.insight: The book says home is now an office, gym, Michelin restaurant, and playground at once; the pandemic-era “boredom of routine” and the itch of wasted time are a brand's way into life at home.

inline.q: Of the book's six pandemic new-normal traits, which three are judged to be lasting, fundamental shifts?
options: Less movement, more time at home, same old routine
Strong e-commerce, remote work, safety gear sales
Strong e-commerce, sweeping promos, instant gratification
Instant gratification, brand loyalty, foot traffic returning
inline.explain: The book names strong e-commerce, sweeping promotions, and instant gratification as fundamental shifts. The first option lists three lifestyle traits during the pandemic.
inline.source: Consumer Resources and Opportunities Hidden in the Pandemic

card.title: Home Is the New Store
card.text: Smaller orders aren't always bad news. Customers may just be coming back more often.

missions.title: Rowing Machines in the Warehouse
missions.brief: Home fitness brand “Steady Legs” has 2,000 unsold rowing machines in the warehouse. Ah-Hao jogs along Rainbow Riverside, waiting to hear a fix that isn't a price cut.

lines.text: {role}, in 2021 our rowers had a three-week wait. Now nobody wants one free.
The boss has exactly one plan: another 30% off.
Do the people who bought them still row?
…Mine's a drying rack now. Rowing alone at home, you're bored in three days.
And a wheelchair user asked if the upper body works. We never pictured that customer.

steps.prompt: How will you help Ah-Hao clear those 2,000 units?

options.text: Go with the boss's 30% off, tie it to Mother's Day, and clear stock first.
options.feedback: The 30%-off window clears 600 units, and the forum starts saying “full-price buyers got played.” For the other 1,400, the boss says next round is 40% off.
options.insight: The book notes that part of pandemic-era demand was driven by promotions. Beyond the book: if you never find consumers' real motivation, demand vanishes the moment buying power pulls back.

options.text: Co-create across industries: scheduled online classes with coaches; rower, gear, and classes as one.
options.feedback: The first class runs at 8 PM, and the coach calls everyone by nickname. Ah-Hao says support now gets calls like “When does my machine arrive? I can't miss class.”
options.insight: The book finds two forces get people to the gym: scheduled classes and socializing. Find striking insights in people, events, time, place, and things, co-create across industries, and consumers will gladly bring the gym home.

options.text: Start with the overlooked: seated upper-body classes with therapists, so wheelchair users can join.
options.feedback: The first demo video is shot by the customer who wrote in. Volume is small, but three rehab clinics ask about group orders. Ah-Hao calls it his proudest call this year.
options.insight: The book's 5I thinking flags “Inequality”: don't let brand interests divide people; give everyone willing a chance to engage with the brand. The 2000s generation of 2030 seeks diversity, equity, and inclusion.

inline.q: “Break the Rules, Co-Create the Ecosystem” separates needs, wants, and demands. How does the book define “demand”?
options: A basic human need, shown as a shortage
Expectations shaped by history, culture, and events
A desire that brands create through ads
inline.explain: The book says needs are basic necessities, wants are expectations shaped by culture and events, and demand is a want backed by buying power.
inline.source: Break the Rules, Co-Create the Ecosystem

card.title: Sell a Reason to Keep Going
card.text: Moving the gear home is easy. Bring the coach and friends home too, and it sells.

missions.title: Ama Wants a Real Person
missions.brief: A telecom wants all-AI customer service, and wants Ama in an ad for its “Active Seniors Plan.” Outside the general store, her phone's bot has misheard her three times.

lines.text: Kiddo, good timing. This robot keeps telling me, “Please state your request.”
I said I want to change my billing address. It offered me a binge-watching plan.
The company also wants you in an ad. It's called the “Active Seniors Plan.”
Active seniors, what's that? I use LINE just fine. I only want to talk to a person.
You ad people are so good at imagining the future, right? So in the future, nobody talks?

steps.prompt: The telecom finalizes tomorrow. What's your answer?

options.text: All-AI service saves on staff; spend the budget on an Ama ad pitched as “tech can be warm too.”
options.feedback: The ad looks great. One comment says, “So warm, but call support and you still get a robot.” Ama watches it and says only, “That person isn't me.”
options.insight: The book's “Human Touch” trend says the more tech spreads, the more real human contact is worth; by 2030, brands should turn to face-to-face interaction.

options.text: AI takes simple issues, one tap reaches a human; the ad is about life and hobbies, no age labels.
options.feedback: The telecom's support head crunches costs, then keeps 20 human agents. Ama calls once: address fixed in three minutes, and she asks about her grandkid's internet plan.
options.insight: The book cites a survey: 67% of consumers want to talk to a person when complaining, and 79% of baby boomers do. Seniors dislike being called “old,” so brands must watch how labels cut both ways.

options.text: Don't rush it: use the four 2030 areas to re-map this company's customers for the next ten years.
options.feedback: You pull an all-nighter on a 4x3 trend matrix. The client's chief strategy officer loves it and wants it for the board. Customer service waits for the next meeting.
options.insight: The book splits 2030 into four areas (universal advocacy, synthetic society, brand offensive, human essence), three trends each; people born in 2000 will be 30 then, the core of spending.

inline.q: In the book's “Human Touch” trend, what share of baby boomers want to talk to a real person when complaining?
inline.explain: It's 67% for all consumers, and 79% of baby boomers agree.

card.title: Real People Are 2030's Luxury
card.text: The smarter tech gets, the more it's worth to talk straight to a person.

missions.title: Which One Gives You Goosebumps
missions.brief: An insurer has two ads but one TV slot. A vendor says its AI emotion reader can spot the hit from viewers' faces. Ms. Su meets you at the Big Dawn Dome Broadcast Center.

lines.text: {role}, Ad A: Dad gives his daughter away. Ad B: an adjuster in the ER at midnight.
The client asked me if TV still works. I said yes, but first you pick which one airs.
That emotion system, can it tell who'll buy insurance?
It sees who frowns, who smiles. Ad A viewers get excited. Ad B viewers go quiet.
Does quiet mean moved, or bored? The machine won't tell you.

steps.prompt: It has to go to air tomorrow. How do you pick?

options.text: Trust the emotion data: go with Ad A and its bigger swings, on TV and online at once.
options.feedback: Ad A's online completion rate looks great, but support calls don't go up. The client asks: everyone's so happy, so why is nobody asking about policies?
options.insight: The book covers emotion-recognition tech like Affectiva, which detects viewers' emotions across creative assets to guide optimization. Beyond the book: it measures emotion, not trust.

options.text: Add a 20-person live panel to the results, ask who the ads made them think of, then decide.
options.feedback: A panelist recalls his dad's hospital stay, when an adjuster rushed papers to the ER at midnight. Ad B airs; the shot people share is the adjuster handing over tissues.
options.insight: The book says media is ultimately a tool, an amplifier with “trust” at its core; the media economy moved from traffic to content to influencers to trust, stacking layer on layer, not replacing.

options.text: Skip choosing: run both online only and let clicks decide whether to buy TV.
options.feedback: After two weeks, Ad A clicks a bit higher. The client drops TV; Ms. Su's sales sheet loses a row. Three months later, a brand recall survey: nobody remembers either ad.
options.insight: The book says newspapers don't replace books, TV doesn't replace newspapers, and the internet won't replace TV; messages overlap across media, so watching one platform's numbers misses things.

inline.q: “Media Tech Always Comes from Human Nature” splits the media economy into 1.0 through 4.0. Which economy is 4.0?
inline.explain: The book's sequence: traffic, content, influencer, then trust. The 4.0 trust economy is “believe first, verify later,” stacked on the first three, not replacing them.
inline.source: Media Tech Always Comes from Human Nature

card.title: Media Amplifies Trust
card.text: Machines can measure a heartbeat, not who this ad made someone think of.

missions.title: The Regulars' Book vs. a CDP
missions.brief: A tech firm is pitching Auntie Hsiu-chin a member data platform that costs more a month than her rent. She sets down her worn regulars' book: what's the difference?

lines.text: The salesman says cookies are gone, and if I don't buy his platform I'll be left behind.
I don't even know if his Cookie is the kind you eat.
That regulars' book of yours. How many people are in it?
Forty-some. Who wants eggs well-done, who wants milk tea, no ice. I remember it all.
Half my business is those forty. The rest? The delivery app won't give me their data.

steps.prompt: How should Auntie Hsiu-chin start a membership program?

options.text: Buy the platform: half off year one; hook up delivery, QR, and LINE data now, no patching later.
options.feedback: Auntie Hsiu-chin texts a deal; traffic jumps 20%. “How'd you get my number?” a regular asks. Later, reports baffle her, full fees hit, and regulars stay in the book.
options.insight: The book says new tech sparks blind, “idol worship” hype; adopt it without planning staff or clear business goals, and you sink into a data swamp.

options.text: Start with those forty regulars: add the shop on LINE, it remembers your order, ready with no wait.
options.feedback: Thirty join in week one. A regular no longer has to repeat “eggs well-done, light sauce” each morning. Auntie Hsiu-chin puts the book in a drawer, but doesn't toss it.
options.insight: The book suggests using the 80/20 rule to start with the most important group, and giving consumers fair perks like convenience, uniqueness, or discounts, so interaction costs stay low and data builds up well.

options.text: Build her own member ID: phone number as account, tying delivery, in-store, and LINE to one person.
options.feedback: Two nights typing the book into a spreadsheet keyed to phone numbers. It's crude, but now she sees one regular order delivery mornings and buy egg crepes in-store later.
options.insight: The book outlines three camps after third-party cookies exit: FLoC, Unified ID 2.0, and first-party tracking. It urges brands to build their own identity graph, from anonymous to partial to full identification.

inline.q: In “The New Identity Revolution,” Unified ID 2.0 generates an encrypted ad ID based on what?
options: Rarely changing values, like an email address
inline.explain: Unified ID 2.0 has an intermediary generate an encrypted ID from stable values like email; the one that groups people by interest is FLoC.

card.title: First-Party Data: Regulars First
card.text: Find the most important 20% first, and give them a reason to share their data.

missions.title: The 38K-Follower “Small” Account
missions.brief: Oat drink brand “Peaceful Oats” got called out by a 38K-follower eco account for petrochemical backing. On Ting-ting's screen, a new comment lands every ten seconds.

lines.text: {role}, help. That account has just 38K followers, and shares already passed 10K.
The client says they're too small to matter. Ignore it, it'll blow over in two days.
Is the investment thing true?
Yeah, one deal last year. But our oats really do use less water.
Lots of commenters say they drink oat milk not for the taste, but because they believe.

steps.prompt: The client is waiting on your call. How do you handle it?

options.text: Stay quiet: don't respond, boost ads for the new flavor, and drown out the noise.
options.feedback: Under the new-flavor ad, the first comment links to that post. Ting-ting spends the whole weekend hiding comments until her fingers cramp.
options.insight: The book cites Oatly: an IG eco influencer with under 40K followers exposed oil-linked investment, and a boycott followed. In an age of values-driven buying, consumers hold the mic.

options.text: Respond openly: admit the investment, explain the money and carbon data, invite the account owner.
options.feedback: The boss hesitates all afternoon, then nods. The account owner visits and posts, “Still doubtful, but they showed me.” Comments turn to arguments, but about substance.
options.insight: The book says Gen Z prefers fact-checking and firsthand experience to form its own view of a brand. Beyond the book: what a brand can do is hold up to scrutiny.

options.text: Split the audience: use social data to find what each values group cares about, and answer each one.
options.feedback: You and the data team work past midnight: vegetarians care about the investment, gym-goers about protein, baristas about foam. Three separate replies; things slowly cool.
options.insight: The book cites a 2020 VICE survey: young people define themselves by personality (65%), values (65%), and interests (58%). Millennials are different to belong to a group; Gen Z finds its group by being different.

inline.q: How does “Value-Driven Consumption” tell apart millennials' and Gen Z's reasons for being “different”?
options: Millennials differ to belong; Gen Z belongs by being different
Millennials chase low prices; Gen Z chases brand image
Millennials care about values; Gen Z only about function
Both differ to outdo their peers
inline.explain: The book says millennials are different for the sake of group identity, while Gen Z finds group identity by being different.
inline.source: Value-Driven Consumption: Brand Communication Strategy Amid Fragmented, Diverse Identities

card.title: Small Accounts Aren't Small
card.text: In the age of values-driven buying, under 50K followers can still get a brand boycotted.

missions.title: The Glowing Runner
missions.brief: A sports drink client rented running ad jerseys for the MRT City Hall Station area. Ah-Kun's back screen is lit, but the client hasn't decided where to run or for whom.

lines.text: {role}, this shirt has GPS and a camera, and it can tell who's in front of me.
The client says everyone's glued to their phones, so give them something to see offline.
Then why not just buy mobile ads?
They say people scroll past phone ads and forget. But on the street, people high-five me.
Problem is, I've only got two legs. Where I run tonight, where I stop: you decide.

steps.prompt: How do you plan tonight's running route?

options.text: Loop the City Hall Station exits all night. More people, more impressions.
options.feedback: Three groups snap and post Ah-Kun, one complaining he's blocking the exit. Impressions look great. The client asks: so how many actually bought?
options.insight: The book says offline big data is precise, broad, and OMO. Beyond the book: chasing crowds wastes the jersey's ability to spot target audiences.

options.text: Use foot-traffic data: the riverside entrance full of after-work runners, then samples at a store.
options.feedback: Ah-Kun stops 15 minutes at the riverside entrance and runs two kilometers with a night-run club. Next day, three nearby stores redeem twice as many samples as elsewhere.
options.insight: The book says Taiwanese spend nearly 8 hours a day online, so physical experiences stand out; Dentsu One's running ad jersey pairs beacons with face recognition to sense target customers and pick what to play.

options.text: The run is just the start: a night-run app where people sign up, run along, and become members.
options.feedback: The app takes three rushed weeks; the first group run draws 120 people. The client says it beats the jersey itself. You say that's because you haven't slept in weeks.
options.insight: The book cites Grab, which went from car rides to delivery and payments, building an ecosystem on user insight; in a survey, over a third of people would consider handling all daily needs through a single brand's services.

inline.q: In “Brand Apocalypse Now,” which plan did Shopify's CEO say he had to scrap during the pandemic?
inline.explain: Shopify's pandemic growth beat the past decade. The CEO said what he expected in ten years had already arrived, so he had to scrap the ten-year plan for 2030.
inline.source: Brand Apocalypse Now: The Era of Customer Experience Innovation

card.title: Offline Is Data Too
card.text: People spend eight hours a day online. The rest of the time deserves a good encounter.

missions.title: Department Stores Sell Ads Now
missions.brief: Shin Kong Mitsuki launched member media: ads in its app, on e-invoices, and on counter screens. A skincare client asks you: move budget over, or keep it in search ads?

lines.text: {role}, we have 800K members' purchase data. Target people who just bought skincare.
Reports show who saw the ad and who paid at the counter. Nobody else can give you that.
Half the client's budget is in search ads now, and results are decent.
Search knows what people want to find. We know what they actually bought.
Oh, and the client's site member data is split across three departments. Nobody shares.

steps.prompt: How do you split the client's budget next quarter?

options.text: Move half to the store's member media. Ads traceable to checkout are easy to justify to the boss.
options.feedback: Counter sales clearly rise in month one. Wen-wen is happy, the client is happy, until they realize most buyers were loyal customers who'd have bought again anyway.
options.insight: The book says retailers are becoming media companies and brands their clients; retail media makes the link between ads and sales clearer, but brands should seek self-serve platforms with transparent pricing and inventory.

options.text: Stay in search for now: sort terms by journey stage to see if shoppers stall at comparing or buying.
options.feedback: You sort 3,000 keywords into five groups. People search hard for “ingredients,” yet the client's site has no ingredients page. Next week: add the page, then talk budget.
options.insight: The book uses five ISRPE stages to decode search: learning something new, seeking solutions, comparing options, buying, sharing experiences. Re-sorting search terms by timing and need reveals intent.

options.text: Get your house in order: merge three departments' member data into one platform, then decide.
options.feedback: Four cross-team meetings; at the third, a door slams. At the fourth, the three heads agree to share one list. Budget unchanged, but next quarter's talks have a basis.
options.insight: The book says the pandemic pushed online shopping 5 years ahead, yet data sits scattered across departments; integration platforms like the cloud and a CDP must connect them, centered on customer experience.

inline.q: “Retail Media: The Next Wave of Emerging Media Is Here” says how do brands and retailers change once a retail media ecosystem forms?
inline.explain: The book says that in retail media, brands play the role of the retailer's client.

card.title: Stores Become Media
card.text: Retailers know what people bought. Figure out what you know first, then decide whose ad slots to buy.
